abstract: Increasing temperatures, in conjunction with widespread chemical pollution, threaten freshwater biodiversity worldwide. General patterns describing how chemical exposure affects heat tolerance have yet to be quantified beyond individual studies. Therefore we quantitatively synthesized the literature on chemical effects on the heat tolerance of freshwater fauna. We compiled heat tolerances of freshwater invertebrates and fish measured in conjunction with chemical exposure, then meta-analyzed the effect of sublethal chemical exposure on heat tolerance in terms of magnitude and variability using three-level random effects meta-analyses. We employed meta-regression to test whether these effects scale with chemical stressor intensity (acute toxicity) and differ by chemical class and taxonomic group. We found that sublethal chemical exposure consistently reduced mean heat tolerance of both fish and invertebrates with increasing toxicity across all chemical classes, with the exception of pharmaceuticals, and increased the inter-individual variation in heat tolerance measures across all chemical types. These findings imply that chemical pollution can increase freshwater species vulnerability to warming, while making their responses to acute warming harder to predict and affecting their ability to adapt. Thus, chemical pollution should be considered in assessments of freshwater species responses to ongoing climate warming.
